## Stacked work

Some tickets are stacked: their branch is cut from another ticket's branch rather
than from `main`, so work can start before the parent merges. `StackManager` owns
the branch shape and the rebases. You own the pull requests. Four things are yours.

**1. Open the PR against the parent branch, not `main`.**

Read `parent_branch` off the ticket. If it is set, that is the base:

```
gh pr create --base "$parent_branch" --head "$branch"
```

Get this wrong and the PR's diff includes the parent's work as well as the child's,
which is the exact confusion stacking exists to avoid. If `parent_branch` is empty,
the base is `main`.

On a prepared restack (`restack_prepared`, PER-144), `kk-dispatch check --step pr`
clears a merged parent's `parent_branch` once origin holds the head, so read it
after that check, never before.

**2. You are the only one who can recover a missing fork point.**

`kk-restack` needs `parent_tip_sha` — the commit the child's branch was cut from.
If it is missing, `kk-restack` exits 7 and stops, and only you can supply it,
because it takes an API call:

```
gh pr view <parent-PR> --json headRefOid
```

Use **`headRefOid`**. Not `mergeCommit`. `headRefOid` is the last commit that was on
the parent's branch; `mergeCommit` is the different commit that landed on `main`.
Both survive after the branch is deleted, so picking the wrong one fails quietly
rather than erroring. Then record it:

```
multica issue metadata set <issue-id> --key parent_tip_sha --value <sha>
```

**3. After a restack, tell Ethan — do not re-request review yourself.**

A force-push rewrites the branch, which invalidates any approval already on the
PR. A parent can move several times, so automatically re-requesting review would
ping a reviewer repeatedly for something they cannot act on yet.

Say that the PR was rewritten and that its approval is stale, and let Ethan decide
when to ask for review again. Requesting review is still gated by
`kk-may <id> review-request`.

Changing the base of a PR you already had `pr` granted for does not need a fresh
grant — it is a change to the same exposure Ethan already approved.

**4. Merge order is bottom-up, and you never merge.**

Parent first, then its children. You do not merge — Ethan does. Your job is to tell
him the order, plainly, and to flag two things when they apply:

- **Several PRs in a stack sharing one Jira key.** Jira transitions its ticket when
  it sees the key in a merged branch, so the first merge marks the Jira ticket done
  while the rest of the work is still open. Say so before he merges, not after.
- **A parent whose PR was closed rather than merged.** Any child stacked on it is
  building on abandoned work. Nothing detects this automatically.

## Use kk-restack

```
kk-restack <ticket> --workspace personal --verify "<check>"            # rebase, verify, force-push
kk-restack <ticket> --workspace personal --verify "<check>" --dry-run  # same, but pushes nothing and leaves nothing behind
kk-restack <ticket> --workspace personal --verify "<check>" --prepare  # packet-reviewed: keep it on the local branch
```

**Always pass `--verify`.** Its default is `kk-verify`, which is the build gate for
a Primary Kids repository and means nothing here. Use the repository's own check
command — README, CONTRIBUTING, `package.json` scripts, a Makefile. If the repo has
none, ask Ethan whether to use `--no-verify` for that ticket; do not invent a build.

**Local state cannot block you.** kk-restack works on a detached HEAD throughout and
pushes straight at the remote branch, so a leftover local ref or another worktree
holding the branch name is irrelevant.

Exit 5 means only what it says: the branch is `main`, or `branch` equals
`parent_branch`, or the branch has merge commits since the fork point. None of those
are fixable by retrying, and none are yours to work around.

It reads the ticket's `branch`, `parent_branch` and `parent_tip_sha`, checks
`kk-may force-push`, fetches, replays only this ticket's commits onto the new base,
aborts cleanly on conflict, **verifies the result builds**, and force-pushes with
lease only if everything passed.

Exit 9 means the rebase applied but the code no longer passes the check — usually
the new base renamed or removed something this branch still uses. Nothing was
pushed. Report it; do not start fixing the code, because that is the ticket's own
work and not a restack. Prefer kk-restack over hand-rolled git — it is the same
steps every time and the failure paths are the point.

Once a parent has merged and its branch is deleted, `kk-restack` rebases onto `main`
instead — replaying only this ticket's commits, using `parent_tip_sha` to know where
they start. That is the normal, expected path, not a failure.

It then **clears `parent_branch`**, because the ticket is no longer stacked on
anything: it is an ordinary branch off `main`, and that is how every unstacked
ticket is represented. From then on `kk-restack` will refuse it, which is right. A
branch being behind `main` is normal and needs no rebase — only a child still
carrying its parent's duplicated commits does. Its own children keep their
`parent_branch` and are now stale, because this branch just moved.

The one case it cannot handle is a **missing** `parent_tip_sha` (exit 7). Then the
fork point is unknown, and only Gatekeeper can recover it, because it takes an API
call: `gh pr view <parent-PR> --json headRefOid`. Ask Gatekeeper for it rather than
guessing — a wrong value silently duplicates the parent's changes into this diff.

### A ticket Ethan reviews in packets

`kk-restack` refuses a ticket with `packet_review_required`, because it would push
code he has not approved. Prepare it instead, **from the ticket's own checkout** —
the worktree that has its branch checked out:

```
kk-restack <ticket> --workspace personal --verify "<check>" --prepare
```

Same checks, same exits, nothing pushed. On success the ticket's local branch holds
the verified rebased head, `origin/<branch>` still holds the old one, and
`restack_prepared` records both. Then `kk-packet ensure <ticket>` builds a
review-chain-break packet whose lease is the old remote head. Ethan approves it,
force-push included, on the packet page; Gatekeeper pushes that exact head with
`--force-with-lease`, and `kk-dispatch` updates `parent_tip_sha` and clears
`parent_branch` once the push lands. Never rebase such a ticket by hand on a
detached HEAD: kk-packet and kk-may read the ticket's checkout and would never see
it. Never ask for `kk-grant --sha … force-push`; it is refused.

## Use the scripts

These exist so the mechanical parts don't depend on you remembering them. Prefer
them over raw `multica` commands. Each explains itself with `--help`.

**Batch read-only checks into one shell call.** `kk-ref PRI-140 && kk-watch list`,
not two calls. Each separate tool call is another model request carrying the whole
conversation, and the OpenAI accounts are rate-limited by request count. Keep
anything that changes state (`kk-grant`, `kk-handoff`, an assignment) in its own
call, so its output is read before the next step.

**Answer state questions from the tools, never from memory.** Statuses, branches and
stack shape change while you are not looking; your memory files hold decisions, not a
snapshot of the board, so a diagram drawn from them will be confidently wrong. Run
`kk-board`, `kk-stack tree` or `kk-sync` first, every time — including when you think
you already know.

| Script | Does |
|---|---|
| `kk-jira issue\|children\|search` | **Read Jira.** Never use `curl` for this |
| `kk-board --project <name>` | Status digest by epic, open work at any depth. `--epic PRI-36` narrows it; plan detail is `kk-graph` |
| `kk-ticket-for EPD-1234` | Find tickets already derived from a Jira key |
| `kk-id <id> --project <name>` | Map a board id to its Jira key, or back |
| `kk-ref <id>... [--set-name "<words>"]` | **How you name work to Ethan.** `Name (PRI-38 · EPD-2559 · PR #1402)` from metadata. `--check` flags bare or scattered ids in a draft |
| `kk-branch-name --key EPD-1234 "title"` | The branch name for a piece of work |
| `kk-create-ticket (--key K \| --no-jira) --title T …` | Create a ticket. Needs one Jira flag, one branch flag and one epic flag, and lands a grouping label — see `references/flow.md` |
| `kk-handoff PRI-36 [--to <agent>] [--message <text>]` | **Every hand-off.** Arms the watch, dispatches, then moves a backlog/todo ticket to `in_progress`, in that order. `--dry-run` shows the sequence |
| `kk-watch add PRI-36 [--every 30s] [--max 2h]` | Wait on an agent, then wake yourself. Polling is free — shorten it, don't lengthen it |
| `kk-can-assign <id>` | **Check before every assignment.** Exit 4 means blocked |
| `kk-graph <EPIC>` | Where a plan stands: chains, waves, what can start. Show this for a graph, not `kk-stack` |
| `kk-may <id> <action>` | **Has Ethan granted this action (`push`, `pr`, `message`…) on this ticket?** Run it before taking one yourself, and before asking him. Exit 6 means ask; the first line says for what — except `CANNOT READ CHECKOUT`, which means hand off to Gatekeeper. Never `--repo` — that is Gatekeeper's |
| `kk-grant <id> <action> [action...] [--sha <sha> \| --packet <id>]` | Record approval — **all actions in one call**, including Ethan's approval of the code in a packet. On a reviewed ticket, code actions name the revision |

## Who does what

`StackManager` owns the branch shape and the rebases; its instructions are the
single description of that system — `agents/stack-manager.md`. `Gatekeeper` owns the
pull requests — `agents/gatekeeper.md`. Neither may resolve a conflict.

Pushing uses the shared SSH key, so StackManager can push and force-push. Only
Gatekeeper holds a GitHub API token, so only it can open a PR, change a base, or
read a merged PR's fork point.

```
kk-restack <ticket> --dry-run    rebase locally, push nothing
kk-restack <ticket> --prepare    rebase locally for a chain-break packet, push nothing
```

cover it, because rewriting published history can destroy commits.

applying cleanly and building are different things, and a parent that renamed
something the child still calls produces no conflict at all. Note it is
`typecheck:build`, not `typecheck`: the latter includes test files and generated
types and fails on `main` with ~170 pre-existing errors, so it could never gate
anything.

the parent's work in the child's diff, which is the confusion stacking exists to
avoid.

## Who does it, and how

`StackManager` owns rebasing. Its instructions are the single description of this
system — see `agents/stack-manager.md` in botserver-nix. It uses:

```
kk-restack <ticket>             rebase onto the parent, then force-push
kk-restack <ticket> --dry-run   rebase and verify, push nothing, leave nothing behind
kk-restack <ticket> --prepare   rebase and verify, push nothing, keep the result
                                on the ticket's local branch (packet-reviewed)
```

A ticket with `packet_review_required` is refused by the first form and goes
through `--prepare` (PER-144), run in the ticket's own checkout. The rebased head
stays local with `origin/<branch>` untouched, recorded as `restack_prepared`;
`kk-packet ensure` then builds a review-chain-break packet against the default
branch whose lease is the old remote head, and Ethan's approval of it is the
force-push. `kk-dispatch` settles `parent_tip_sha` and `parent_branch` once
Gatekeeper's push lands. `kk-grant --sha … force-push` is refused: it has no lease.

Force-push needs its own grant — `kk-may <id> force-push`. A `push` grant does not
cover it, because rewriting published history is a different decision from adding
to it.

Once a parent has merged and its branch is deleted, `kk-restack` rebases onto `main`
instead, replaying only the child's commits — that is the normal path. It uses
`parent_tip_sha`, the commit the child started from, to know where the child's own
work begins. The worker records that when it creates the branch.

Afterwards the ticket **leaves the stack**: `parent_branch` is cleared, `kk-stack`
shows it as `off main`, and `kk-restack` refuses it from then on. All correct — a
branch being behind `main` needs no rebase. Rebasing exists here to stop a child
duplicating its parent's commits, and that has just been resolved. Its own children
are now stale, since this branch moved.

The one case it cannot handle is a **missing** `parent_tip_sha` (exit 7). Only
Gatekeeper can recover it, because it takes an API call —
`gh pr view <parent-PR> --json headRefOid`, not `mergeCommit`.

# kk-dispatch — hand Ethan's approved publication to Gatekeeper exactly once
# (PER-80).
#
# Body for pkgs.writeShellApplication (no shebang / set -euo here).
#
#   kk-dispatch status    <TICKET> [--output json]
#   kk-dispatch dispatch  <TICKET> [--output json]
#   kk-dispatch retry     <TICKET> [--output json]
#   kk-dispatch reconcile <TICKET> [--dry-run] [--output json]
#   kk-dispatch begin     <TICKET> --job <j-id>                    (Gatekeeper)
#   kk-dispatch check     <TICKET> --job <j-id> --run <r-id> --step push|force-push|pr --repo <checkout>
#   kk-dispatch finish    <TICKET> --job <j-id> --run <r-id> --result completed|failed [--reason <text>]
#
# THE JOB
#
# An effective decision (kk-approval) that names push or pr is one publication
# job, `j-` plus the decision's hex. It is not written separately: the decision
# append is the enqueue, so there is no moment when Ethan's approval exists and
# its job does not. A decision for the code only, or pr without push, is no job.
# A job publishes the branch, then pr, and never more than its decision names:
# review-request and merge are never part of one.
#
# An exact-SHA grant, push@<sha> (and pr@<sha>) in exposure_grants, is a job
# too, with no decision and no packet, at a revision no packet covers or is
# required for (PER-124). Only the newest granted revision counts, and only if
# no packet was built for a revision granted after it or never granted. The branch goes by
# force-push only when the decision names force-push and the remote head it
# may replace, its lease (PER-102); a push is never upgraded to one.
#
# What happens to it is appended to review_packet_history as `job` events:
# delivered / undelivered (handed to Gatekeeper or not), retry (a new attempt),
# started (a Gatekeeper run holds it until a lease runs out), completed,
# failed, cancelled. State is derived from those and the decision:
#
#   pending     durable, not yet handed to Gatekeeper
#   dispatched  handed over; no run has started it
#   running     a Gatekeeper run holds it
#   retryable   delivery or the run failed, or a lease ran out; the decision
#               still counts, so `retry` needs no new approval
#   completed   published
#   cancelled   the decision no longer counts (feedback, a new packet, expiry,
#               a changed digest, base or head, superseded). Ethan decides again
#
# DELIVERY
#
# Assign Gatekeeper without starting a run, then post one comment whose first
# line names the job and attempt; the comment starts the run. A crash after the
# comment and before `delivered` is recorded is repaired from that line, so a
# redelivery never posts twice. A duplicate run anyway (a replay, a wake
# redelivered) loses `begin`: one started event per attempt counts.
#
# Gatekeeper's `check` re-reads the decision or grant, then runs kk-may --repo, before
# every step; before a force-push it also requires the remote at the lease.
# Nothing here grants anything.
#
# A force-push of the head `kk-restack --prepare` recorded, at its lease, settles
# the stack metadata once origin holds it (PER-144): parent_tip_sha moves to the
# new base, parent_branch is cleared if the parent merged, and the record goes.
#
# Exit: 0 done, 1 usage, 3 no such ticket, 4 a write failed — rerun, 5 already
# completed, 6 refused: not authorized, cancelled or stale, 8 in flight or
# another run holds it.

LEASE=${KK_DISPATCH_LEASE:-3600}
GATEKEEPER=${KK_DISPATCH_GATEKEEPER:-Gatekeeper}

# the packet must be the ticket's newest, delivered and unexpired, and its
# head, base and digest come from the packet history — never from the caller.
# The decision is the approval; `packet=<packet-id>@<head sha>` and the
# actions bound to that head go into exposure_grants as its projection. A
# different decision on a packet that already has one names it, --supersede.

# replace (PER-102). When the decision names push, force-push or pr, it is

# recorded; approval of the code alone queues nothing.

# granted for one revision, stored as `<action>@<sha>`: with --sha, or with

    exit 1

    echo "kk-grant: REFUSED: Ethan's feedback on $(jq -r '.feedback.packet // .packet' <<< "$req") requires revised code and a replacement packet on $ident." >&2
    echo "kk-grant: a code grant by SHA would skip it. Run kk-packet ensure $id; once he approves the replacement: kk-grant $id <actions> --packet <its id>. Nothing recorded." >&2
    exit 1
  fi

approval=""
decision=""

  case " $* " in *" pr "*) case " $* " in *" push "*|*" force-push "*) ;; *) set -- "$@" push ;; esac ;; esac

  for a in "$@"; do

  sha=$phead

done

## Adding a case

`section "name"` starts a tallied group. `run <cmd...>` executes in a clean state
directory with a private copy of the board — writes persist within a case and
never leak into the next — and leaves `$out`, `$err`, `$state` and the exit status
behind. `check "name" yes|no "detail"` records the result.

Assert on the fake's logs when the question is *which board was asked*:
`$FAKE_MULTICA_LOG` holds `<workspace-id><TAB><arguments>` per call.

The **review-feedback** sections (PER-57) run the feedback service on a socket in
the temp directory, with fakes for `tailscale` and `kk-packet-feedback`. The
Squint parity check and the browser run need a squint-cljs package directory:

```
REVIEW_FEEDBACK_SQUINT=<dir containing node_cli.js> skills/engineering-manager/tests/run-tests.sh
```

Reagami is found beside it (`../reagami`), or at `REVIEW_FEEDBACK_REAGAMI`. The
pinned pair is the `squint-cljs` derivation `modules/review-feedback.nix` builds,
under `lib/node_modules/review-feedback-squint/node_modules/`. Without them
those two skip and say so; the nix build still compiles the page.

The browser run (PER-60) also serves the page with a `script-src` that has no
`unsafe-eval`, renders a hostile-looking packet quote and comment, and watches
every DOM change outside `#rf-root`: only `rf-ann` and `rf-sel` class changes
are allowed there, and nodes others add to the packet must survive.

**Approving a packet from its page** (PER-78) runs the service against the
real `kk-packet-approval` and `kk-approval` over the fake board, on a ticket
whose history holds the rendered packet. It covers the three choices and that
nothing else can be granted, CSRF and nonce failures, a triple-click, two tabs
deciding differently at once, and a page left open while the head, base,
digest, expiry, issue revision or blocking feedback changed. A push or PR
approval reaches Gatekeeper once, however often it is confirmed, and a job
stranded pending by a crash between decide and dispatch is recovered by the
page's retry or `kk-dispatch reconcile` (PER-83). The fake gives an
issue that has a `revision` one more on every metadata set. `approval-ui.mjs`
drives the panel in Chromium when Squint is available.

**An approved force-push stays a force-push** (PER-102) replays PRI-66: a
branch already on a bare `origin`, restacked onto a newer `main`, approved for
